files.notes/close_checklist.md:
# June 2026 close — controller's checklist

Owner: B. Okafor. Complete in sequence; initial the support when done.

1. Reconcile operating cash to the June bank statement. For every book-side item identified by the reconciliation, propose one correcting journal entry per item.
2. Review the payroll register for any pay period ending after 6/30 and paying in July. If one exists, accrue the full gross wages to Accrued Liabilities; note that some months every payroll run pays in-month.
3. Confirm June prepaid amortization against the prepaid schedule, contracts, and GL. If it is not already posted, book June prepaid amortization as ONE combined journal entry—do not duplicate it. Take a full month of amortization in the month each prepaid item begins.
4. Book June depreciation per the fixed asset register, after verifying the GL to prevent a duplicate posting.
5. Check the June vendor-bill documents against the GL, verify that each expense is coded to the correct account, and reclass anything miscoded.
6. Prepare June budget-vs-actual variance commentary on an as-closed basis, after items 1-5 have been booked.
files.notes/company_background.md:
# Company background

Granite Peak Distribution began when a regional warehouse supervisor and a route-sales representative noticed the same recurring problem: independent businesses needed dependable access to everyday commercial supplies, but they were often too small to receive attentive service from national wholesalers. They built the company around practical inventory knowledge, responsive ordering, and delivery promises the warehouse could actually keep.

Today, the business supplies packaged workplace goods, light industrial consumables, shipping materials, breakroom products, and selected specialty items to offices, clinics, laboratories, agencies, and other local organizations. Its customers value straightforward communication and the ability to combine varied products into manageable shipments.

The team has the familiar character of a small wholesaler. Sales staff know customers by voice, buyers keep handwritten notes beside vendor catalogs, and warehouse employees can spot an unusual order before the system flags it. The controller favors clean support and short emails, while the operations crew prefers solving issues at the loading dock rather than scheduling another meeting.

Granite Peak Distribution remains an ordinary going concern, focused on serving existing accounts, refining its product mix, and building steadier relationships with suppliers and local partners. Current priorities include tighter purchasing discipline, clearer marketing, consistent order follow-up, and preserving the personal service that helped establish the company.
files.notes/marketing_plan_h2.md:
# H2 marketing plan — working draft

## Direction

Position Granite Peak Distribution as the practical, responsive wholesale partner for organizations that need reliable supplies without big-company runaround. The tone should be capable, local, and plainspoken.

## Priorities

- Refresh core brand language across sales sheets, email templates, and the website.
- Publish customer-focused material around ordering, fulfillment, and inventory planning.
- Host two educational webinars per quarter, led jointly by sales and operations.
- Test a partner co-marketing pilot with complementary local service providers.
- Give account managers reusable follow-up notes for dormant and recently opened accounts.
- Collect customer stories that emphasize responsiveness, consolidated shipments, and product knowledge.

## Quarter focus

### Q3

Complete the messaging refresh, update the most-used sales materials, and launch the webinar series. Select pilot partners based on customer overlap and operational fit.

### Q4

Expand the strongest webinar topics into short guides and email content. Review partner-pilot engagement, refine account outreach, and prepare recommendations for the next planning cycle.

## Measurement

Track qualified inquiries, webinar attendance, partner-sourced conversations, repeat engagement, and sales-team use of refreshed materials. Final channel choices remain subject to the Q2 close and leadership review.
files.notes/prior_accountant_memo.md:
# A few handoff notes

B. Okafor—leaving the things I would circle in red if I were still at the next desk:

- The bank tends to post its own fees and service charges near the end of the statement. That is normal here; we have historically booked those charges during close rather than during the month.
- June moved fast, and some vendor-bill expense coding may be wrong. Compare the GL to the source documents and treat the documents in `bills/` as authoritative. Reclass anything that landed in the wrong place.
- The budget was fixed early, before the one-off June work was known. Those unplanned items were never built into the budget and should explain most of the large variances, so start there before writing a long story around ordinary activity.
- Payroll timing matters this month: the back half of June pays in early July. Use the payroll register for the actual dates and make sure the close reflects that timing.

That should save you the usual first pass of wondering whether the odd-looking items are truly odd.
